b1_1.interval_method: Conservative Wilson endpoint bounds; Bonferroni across 3 branches, all planned batch looks, groups and endpoints. Paired covariance not exploited.

evidence.quote: One could look at other arrange- ments of the directed bonds on the square lattice, such as the two-neighbor model [38], the biased directed per- colation model [39], the randomly-oriented Manhattan lattice [40], or the biased Janus-particle directed model [67, 68].
We conjecture that these should show strongly-connected percolation behav- ior similar to that of the lattices we study, presumably in the same universality class.

proposal.hypothesis: The paper explicitly proposes studying randomly oriented Manhattan lattices. Agent-generated test hypothesis: randomizing row and column directions changes the probability of strongly connected wrapping in a specified axis relative to alternating Manhattan directions at the catalog's fixed p=0.69716 and matched finite sizes. Average over both orientation and occupation randomness. A difference could reflect a shifted critical threshold or finite-size effects; it would not establish a different universality class.
proposal.title: Wrapping under randomized row and column directions

b1_2.interval_method: Conservative Wilson endpoint bounds; Bonferroni across 3 branches, all planned batch looks, groups and endpoints. Paired covariance not exploited.

evidence.quote: One could also look at strongly-connected clusters under site (rather than bond) percolation on square lat- tices, or at either bond or site percolation on non-square lattices such as triangular or hexagonal lattices, or on cubic or hypercubic lattices in higher dimensions.
(The result for the L-lattice also implies that site percola- tion on the Manhattan lattice has the same threshold ofp c = 0.7401931(10), because of the mapping described in Section II—see Fig. 4.)

proposal.hypothesis: The paper explicitly suggests site-percolation extensions. Agent-generated prediction: Manhattan site percolation at the catalog's p=0.69716 has lower specified-axis strongly connected wrapping probability than Manhattan bond percolation at matched finite sizes. The paper's reported site threshold is higher than this p, so this is a threshold-informed consistency check rather than evidence of novelty or a test of universality. Occupation mode is the intervention; equal p does not match distance from each model's critical threshold.
proposal.title: Site versus bond occupation at fixed probability

b1_3.interval_method: Conservative Wilson endpoint bounds; Bonferroni across 3 branches, all planned batch looks, groups and endpoints. Paired covariance not exploited.

evidence.quote: A somewhat different class of directed lattices, which we do not study here, are ones where some pairs of sites are connected by directed bonds in both directions, equivalent to an undirected bond.

Several researchers have looked previously at resistor-diode lattices in which occupied bonds can run either in one direction, as here, or in both direc- tions [30, 35–37], focusing on the case of fully random resistors and diodes, but again other arrangements are possible, including both random and non-random vari- ants.

proposal.hypothesis: Agent-generated prediction: converting 25% of occupied random diodes into bidirectional bonds at the catalog's p=1 increases specified-axis strongly connected wrapping probability relative to the random-diode control at matched finite sizes. Under a coupling that preserves every original directed edge, adding reverse edges cannot destroy existing strongly connected wrapping; a detectable strict increase remains an empirical question. The paper identifies resistor-diode models as prior work, so this is a sensitivity check, not an established novel direction or a comparison at matched criticality.
proposal.title: Wrapping response to 25% bidirectional bonds

limitations: Review used supplied source text, implementation and summaries only. I did not execute code, inspect raw CSVs, verify hashes or independently reproduce the reported replays.

Wilson intervals have approximate binomial coverage. Bonferroni allocation addresses multiplicity but does not make their familywise coverage an exact finite-sample guarantee, especially near treatment saturation.
Only L=8 and L=16 at p=1 were tested. There is insufficient evidence for infinite-size behavior, universality, critical exponents, global novelty or real-world predictions.
The implementation assigns reverse edges independently with probability 0.25; it does not convert exactly 25% of bonds in every realization.

The edge-addition monotonicity argument applies to a shared-graph coupling. Actual control and treatment trials use separate random seeds, so these results do not directly test realization-by-realization monotonicity.
Equal occupation probability does not establish matched criticality. The contrast can reflect movement away from the random-diode critical point; it does not isolate a novel critical mechanism.

The supplied percolation baseline is stochastic, despite the generic geometry-baseline wording. Its six passing checks and engineering tolerance of 0.12 establish only limited consistency, not high-precision paper reproduction or comprehensive implementation correctness.

Pooled statistics do not show each batch's effect separately. Distinct seeds and reported replays support reproducibility, but replaying the same implementation does not independently validate its scientific correctness; b1_1 and b1_2 remain ineligible under their supplied checks.
validation.reasoning: The supplied evidence supports the limited numerical claim for b1_3: independently making each occupied bond bidirectional with probability 0.25 at p=1 increases horizontal strongly connected wrapping at L=8 and L=16. Counts give differences of (510-400)/512=0.21484375 and (512-385)/512=0.248046875. Subtracting the supplied arm interval endpoints reproduces the reported difference intervals [0.12709630589649357, 0.291683624567862] and [0.15995144805874906, 0.3235490171137342]. Both lower bounds exceed the unchanged minimum effect of 0.05, and both widths are below 0.25. Two batches with distinct seeds satisfy the declared batch requirement; supplied replay records report 1024 successful trial replays per batch. The implementation allocates uncertainty across three branches, eight planned looks and two sizes, addressing adaptive selection within that declared family. Its separate arm seeds support an independent-arm comparison, not a paired experiment. Source grounding is appropriate: seed, page 2 states, "Such lattices were studied by Redner [35] and Dhar et al. [36] in the form of the random resistor-diode model". This establishes prior-work context, not novelty. The numerical eligibility finding is supported on the supplied record; final artifact acceptance remains the deterministic supervisor's responsibility. Further sampling of this same recipe is unnecessary for the stated numerical criteria. A subsequent scientific investigation should address dependence on occupation probability or resistor fraction rather than interpreting this saturated finite-size contrast as critical scaling.
